title: Source follower
description: A source follower (common-drain buffer): the drain sits at VDD, the source drives the load, and the output tracks the input one gate-source drop below it. The voltage gain $A_v = g_m/(g_m + g_{ds} + 1/R_L)$ is just under unity and the output resistance is about $1/g_m$, so this stage buffers a high-impedance node into a resistive load $R_L$ without voltage gain. The DC level shift is one $V_{GS}$: $V_{out} = V_{in} - V_{GS}$. $V_{GS}$ is not known before sizing, yet the drain-source voltage $V_{DD} - V_{out}$ the device is sized at depends on it, so vgs_est is solved: the engine searches its range for the value that equals the sized device's own $V_{GS}$, and its stored value is never read. The body is assumed tied to the source ($V_{SB} = 0$), so no body effect appears and $g_{mb}$ drops out of the gain. That is an assumption about the layout, not an algebraic convenience: it requires an isolated body — a deep-n-well NMOS, or the PMOS-in-its-own-well version of this stage. On a bulk-grounded device the source-body generator loads the source directly; measured on a sky130 tt realization at these defaults it is about 52 uS against a 240 uS $g_m$, which pulls the gain from 0.95 down to roughly 0.79 and misses the 0.85 target. In a shared well, this sheet does not describe the circuit. The gate is held at $V_{in}$, the input level the application presents, so no gate is a port; the bias current is drawn as an ideal source from the output to ground, and $R_L$ is a small-signal load only, not drawn, so it takes no DC current.

params.name: V_in
params.note: input DC level; the output sits one vgs below it

params.name: R_L
params.note: load resistance at the source, a small-signal load only: the gain and output-resistance equations and the loading check read it, but it is not drawn, so it takes none of the DC bias current. It may be large (a light load approaches Av -> gm/(gm+gds))

params.name: gm_id
params.note: higher gm/ID raises gm (gain closer to 1, lower Rout) at the cost of headroom

params.name: vgs_est
params.note: the follower's gate-source drop, which places its drain-source bias at VDD - V_in + vgs_est. Solved, not retuned: the engine searches for the value that equals the sized device's own vgs, so the stored value is never read, and a table with a different threshold lands somewhere else (near 0.77 V on a sky130 tt nfet at these defaults). It is searched between 0.2 V, below the threshold region, and the 1.8 V supply

equations.name: V_out
equations.note: the DC level shift: the output is one gate-source drop below the input

equations.name: Av
equations.note: follower gain, below unity; gmb is absent because the body is tied to the source. On a bulk-grounded device it belongs in the denominator alongside gds, and costs roughly a sixth of the gain

equations.name: Rout
equations.note: output resistance, about 1/gm for a light load

equations.name: vn_in
equations.note: input-referred channel thermal density; the near-unity gain passes it through with little change

equations.name: cgg_in
equations.note: estimate: the capacitance the input terminal presents — this stage's gate capacitance. The table carries the TOTAL gate capacitance with no gate-drain split, so nothing here can weight the two terminals by how much each one swings. The drain sits at the supply, so there is no Miller multiplication to miss here; what there is instead is bootstrapping — the source follows the gate to within a few percent, taking most of $C_{GS}$ out of the driver's way, so this estimate OVERSTATES what the driver sees. No check reads it

equations.name: I_q
equations.note: estimate: quiescent supply current — the one branch these equations model, set by the bias source under the follower. The datasheet line for comparing designs; no check reads it

checks.note: gm/ID cannot exceed the weak-inversion ceiling of the data
read from the table's own noise where it carries it, and from the γ = 1 estimate otherwise; the simulator owns noise sign-off

the stage is actually buffering only while the load it drives is well above its own output resistance. Ten to one is the convention for that regime, not physics: at exactly ten to one the loaded gain still sits within about ten percent of what an unloaded follower would give, and below it the load, not the device, sets the gain
